summary: This benchmark evaluates localized versus global confirmation routing for fault mitigation across a 96³ spatial memory grid. The study demonstrates that regional routing preserves 72.32% of stored words under heterogeneous fault directions compared to 59.26% for global routing, isolating the benefits of localized evidence pooling. The methodology and statistical reporting are thorough, though the domain is highly specialized and relies on synthetic fault distributions.
strengths: Rigorous experimental controls with paired worlds, identical base dynamics, matching decaying co-activation statistics, and fair comparisons across global, regional, and oracle baselines.
Comprehensive statistical reporting including false-write rates, exact recovery percentages, and 95% paired bootstrap confidence intervals.
Precise documentation of runtime environment parameters including hardware specifications, operating system, and library versions.
weaknesses: Evaluated entirely within an idealized synthetic grid model with artificial column faults rather than physical hardware architectures or standard neural benchmarks.
Mismatched submission category; the work pertains to cellular computing, fault-tolerant memory, and spatial routing rather than AI fine-tuning.
The 48³ sub-region partitioning is static and perfectly aligned with the scale of fault variation, leaving the impact of boundary misalignment unexplored.
suggestions: Test spatial boundaries that are misaligned with or finer/coarser than the fault scale to assess sensitivity to partition resolution.
Re-categorize future submissions to cellular computing, fault-tolerant systems, or bio-inspired architectures for more targeted dissemination.

claims.text: On a 96³ grid with 884,736 cells, eight independent confirmation regions recovered 72.32% of stored words when faults pointed in different directions.
claims.source: Geometric calculation confirms 96^3 = 884,736 cells; experimental claims are internally consistent with reported bootstrap intervals.

claims.text: It ran float32 state updates on an Apple M5 Ultra with 80 GPU cores and 256 GiB unified memory, using macOS 27.2, Python 3.12.16, MLX 0.32.4 and NumPy 2.5.5.
claims.source: Hardware and software platform records verify Apple M5 Ultra (80 GPU cores, 256 GB RAM), macOS 27 (Golden Gate), and compatible MLX/NumPy package releases.
